label: risk management and insurance
overview: Risk management scenarios typically surface when a client has experienced a risk event, is anticipating one, or has no formal framework for identifying and treating the risks threatening their objectives. Risk is defined by the ISO 31000 standard as the effect of uncertainty on objectives — and can produce both negative and positive deviations from what is expected. The advisor's role is to move the client from reactive fire-fighting to a structured process: establish context, identify risks, evaluate their consequence and probability, select the appropriate treatment strategy, and build an action plan with assigned ownership. Insurance is one treatment tool within this framework — not a substitute for the framework itself.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the client responding to a risk event that has already occurred, trying to prevent a foreseeable one, or building a risk management framework from scratch?
diagnostic_entry.risk_event_already_occurred: Establish what happened, what the consequence was, and whether a risk treatment was in place. Use this as the entry point for the 5-step framework — starting at Step 3 (Evaluate) to assess how the event would be classified on the heatmap, then move to Step 4 to determine the correct treatment strategy going forward.
diagnostic_entry.foreseeable_risk_to_prevent: Start at Step 1 (Establish Context) and work through the full 5-step framework. Identify the risk source and the event type before selecting a treatment. Do not jump to insurance or avoidance before the risk has been properly evaluated.
diagnostic_entry.building_framework_from_scratch: Work through all five steps in sequence. Establish the timeframe and categories first, then use SWOT analysis and historical data to identify risks. The Risk Heatmap is the key visual tool for prioritising which risks require immediate treatment versus monitoring.

materials.name: Risk and Uncertainty — Core Theory
materials.summary: Establishes what risk actually is before any process starts. Under ISO 31000 risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives — and that effect can be positive as well as negative. Uncertainty comes from a deficiency of information about future events, so the whole aim of risk management is to reduce it. Transferring risk is not a modern invention; it is a practice that has evolved over four thousand years.
materials.who_when: Clients who treat risk as nothing more than an insurance policy, or who need to understand why a structured process is worth the effort before starting one.
steps: Define risk with the client in the ISO 31000 sense — the effect of uncertainty on objectives — and establish that a deviation can be favourable as well as damaging.
Trace the uncertainty to its source: a deficiency of information or incomplete knowledge about future events and their consequences.
Make risk transfer tangible with the history — Chinese merchants spreading cargo across several vessels so one capsized boat could not ruin them (3rd–2nd millennia BC).
Show risk transfer for a price — Babylonian merchants paying lenders an extra premium to cancel the loan if the shipment was stolen, recorded in the Code of Hammurabi around 1750 BC.
Show risk pooling — the Rhodian 'general average', where merchants pooled funds to reimburse anyone whose goods were jettisoned in a storm.

Show the abstraction into contracts — 14th-century Genoa separated the roles of investor and insurer, letting risk move to dedicated pools and transforming overseas trade into the modern insurance industry.
Land the point: modern frameworks combine those ancient transfer principles with a structured process, then move the client into the five steps.

materials.name: 5-Step Risk Management Framework
materials.summary: The practical process — a systematic application of policies and procedures to identify, evaluate and treat the risks threatening the client's objectives. Every treatment is weighed on cost against certainty of outcome, and every treatment leaves residual risk behind, so the process is continuous rather than a one-off exercise.
materials.who_when: Any client formalising how they handle risk, and any client reviewing their exposure after an incident or a change in their operating environment.
steps: Establish context — set the timeframe the plan covers and the categories for consequence and probability. Weigh external context (local and international environment, stakeholder values, legal trends) against internal context (governance structure, capability, culture).
Identify risks — brainstorm from strategic plans, S.W.O.T. analysis, historical data and expert advice, naming both the risk source it originates from and the events it could produce.
Evaluate risks — assess each one's consequence (how bad the loss could be) and probability (how likely it is), then plot them on a heatmap so visibility and accountability sit with the team.
Compare the result against the client's own risk criteria to decide whether each risk level is tolerable.

Determine the treatment — Accept it as assessed, Avoid it by ceasing the activity, Reduce it by limiting exposure and volume, or Transfer it to a third party through insurance, a cooperative, or a guarantee of limited liability. Judge each on cost and on certainty of outcome.

Develop the action plan — turn treatments into active controls with a named task, a designated Risk Owner who holds the authority and the accountability, and a date. Add contingency and disaster recovery plans where the exposure warrants them.
Monitor the residual risk left after treatment, and keep the whole framework under continual review — controls are checked and observed over time, never set once and forgotten.

advisor_guidance.insurance_is_not_the_framework: The most common client misconception is equating risk management with buying insurance. Insurance is one Transfer tool within Step 4 — it addresses the financial consequence of an event but does nothing to reduce the probability of it occurring. Frame insurance as part of the strategy, not a substitute for having one.
advisor_guidance.residual_risk_must_be_monitored: Risk treatments rarely eliminate risk entirely. After any treatment is applied, residual risk remains. The action plan in Step 5 must include a monitoring mechanism — a scheduled review date and an assigned Risk Owner. Risk management without ongoing monitoring is risk management on paper only.
advisor_guidance.risk_owner_accountability: Every risk on the register must have a named Risk Owner — a person with both the authority and the accountability to manage it. A risk without an owner will not be managed. When presenting the action plan, secure explicit commitment from the client on who owns each risk before leaving.
advisor_guidance.heatmap_creates_shared_visibility: The Risk Heatmap is one of the most effective facilitation tools in the framework. Plotting risks visually on a consequence-versus-probability matrix makes the relative severity of each risk immediately visible to the whole leadership team — creating shared accountability rather than leaving risk assessment in the hands of one person.
advisor_guidance.risk_can_be_positive: Opening the conversation by acknowledging that risk includes positive deviations — not just negative ones — reframes the client's relationship with the topic. A client who sees risk management only as loss prevention misses the upside: a business with well-managed downside risk is better positioned to take calculated upside risks.
